Artist.value: Museum of London, Kate Sumnall, 2007-10-05 11:20:47

ImageDescription.value:
A Medieval decorated square floor tile, ‘Winchester’ type (13th – 14th century). Only part of the tile remains, two corners and part of the body is missing. The front surface is glazed and decorated with a two tone pattern. The pattern comprises a central lozenge-shape in white with a long cross that divides the lozenge into quarters; each arm of the cross has a trilobed terminal. At the centre of the cross is an annulet and in each quarter is a lis with stem that extends into the central annulet. The pattend is entirely in white against a red background.

The pattern is very similar to no. W104 (Betts 2002:58), the pattern on this tile is a slightly larger scale.

Dimensions: length: 107.70mm; width: 86.11mm; thickness: 20.72mm; weight: 224g.

Reference: Betts, I. 2002. Medieval ‘Winchester’ Floor Tiles. MoLAS monograph 11. MoLAS: London.

A Post Medieval London Delftware (tin-glazed earthenware) polychrome floor tile fragment (c.1618-c.1650). This fragment is probably from the Pickleherring pothouse, Southwark. The tile has a hand-painted geometric design of blue on white with a floral motif in the centre and a semicircular corner decorative area in yellow in one corner, there is a tiny area of green paint still visible in the adjacent corner.

The tile is very similar to another corner fragment from Pickleherring pothouse; Pickleherring Design 11, Style 1 (Tyler, Betts & Stephenson 2008:54-5). The differences can be explained by variation in the hand-painting.

Artist.value: Museum of London, Kate Sumnall, 2013-05-28 09:47:38

ImageDescription.value:
A Post Medieval ceramic fragment of a London Delftware (tin-glazed earthenware) polychrome floor tile (c.1618-c.1660). The fragment includes one corner of the decorated 'medallion' style tile. Originally the tile was square, only one corner remains now. Similar examples within the Museum of London collections depict natural scenes of animals and birds stood on grass. Presumably this tile has a similarly natural scene, although it may be anthropomorphic. The surviving fragment includes part of a central motif painted in yellow/green with blue outline against a blue and white background but there is not enough surviving to identify the subject. This is enclosed within a circular border of blue, white and purple concentric rings against a blue background with a blue and white geometric pattern in the corner.

The tile is similar to others illustrated in Tyler, Betts & Stephenson (2008:54-5) and ones recorded on the Portable Antiquities Scheme database e.g. LON-D960D7; LON-6A3247; LON-306A43

Roy Stephenson has examined this fragment and suggested that it was made at the Rothehithe pottery in London and dates to c. 1640 to 1660 AD.

Dimensions: weight: 185g.

Reference: Tyler, K., Betts, I. And Stephenson, R. 2008. London's Delftware Industry. The tin-glazed pottery industries of Southwark and Lambeth. MoLAS Monograph 40. Identification by Ian Betts, Building Material Specialist, Museum of London Archaeology Service.

75086433.title: File:An incomplete Medieval to Post Medieval two-colour, 'Lewes' group glazed ceramic floor tile dating to the third quarter of the 14th century. (FindID 850976).jpg

ObjectName.value: An incomplete Medieval to Post Medieval two-colour, 'Lewes' group glazed ceramic floor tile dating to the third quarter of the 14th century.

Categories.value: Portable Antiquities Scheme|Images uploaded by Fæ|Portable Antiquities Scheme, LON|Files with coordinates missing SDC location of creation (51° N, 1° W)|Photographs by Stuart Wyatt

Artist.value: The Portable Antiquities Scheme, Stuart Wyatt, 2017-06-06 12:01:13

ImageDescription.value:
An incomplete Medieval two-colour, 'Lewes' group glazed ceramic floor tile dating to the third quarter of the 14th century. This is an Eames design No. 2180 examples in the catalogue are no. 11,284 and 13,463. The tile has a large fleur de lis within a lozenge at its centre with decorative geometric motifs at each corner. This tile formed one element from a patterned pavement where adjacent tiles would have completed the geometric corner motifs. One corner in missing and the other three corners of this tile are badly abraded. The tile is a highly fired, bright red ceramic.

Dimensions: length: 101.55mm; width: 102.26mm; maximum thickness: 21.58mm; weight: 326g.

An example of this tile can be seen in the Museum of London online collection ID: 84.9/3. Another two-colour floor tile with fleur de lis on the database is LON-1EC2B4.

Eames (1980:209-10) writes "A small group of two-colour tiles, found mainly in Sussex, was identified by Lord Ponsonby of Shulbrede and termed the 'Lewes' group." she continues "They were certainly used in London. There is a tile from the City of London in the private museum of Langley (London) Ltd., Borough High Street, Southwark, decorated with design 2180."

Eames (1980:210) writes "A date in the third quarter of the 14th century is suggested by the presence of these tiles in Poynings church, which was built in 1368. Such a date would be possible for all of the decorative motifs present."

Reference: Eames E., 1980. Catalogue of medieval lead-glazed earthenware tiles in the department of Medieval and Later Antiquities, British Museum, vol. I & II. London: British Museum Publications.

ObjectName.value: Courtyard Tiles and Stonework in Sintra, Portugal (54932333697)

Categories.value: Files with coordinates missing SDC location of creation|Flickr images reviewed by FlickreviewR 2|Cloister of Palácio Nacional da Pena|Flickr images missing SDC published in

ImageDescription.value:
This courtyard in Sintra has a way of pulling you into its rhythm—tile, stone, shadow, repeat. The geometric azulejos shift in pattern as your eye scans the walls, each band revealing a different language of color and symmetry. Green and gold rosettes sit beneath cooler blue-and-white grids, all anchored by the soft, time-worn pink of the columns. The architecture bends toward both intimacy and ornament, as if the builders wanted to create a space that feels both sheltered and endlessly detailed.

Carved stone faces and animal forms watch over the upper walkway, adding that unmistakable Sintra strangeness—mythic without being theatrical, decorative without being fragile. The warm afternoon light hits the courtyard at an angle that deepens the relief of the stonework, making the arches feel even more sculptural. Everything here seems crafted to make you linger: the patterned tile floor pulling you inward, the arches framing layers of shadow, the small potted plants adding that touch of life to all the texture and geometry.

It’s the kind of place where you stand still and feel the centuries around you—not as history frozen in place, but as something living, carried forward through craft, color, and care.

Credit.value: Courtyard Tiles and Stonework in Sintra, Portugal

Artist.value: Dale Cruse - 10M views from San Francisco, CA, USA

ImageDescription.value: This photograph captures the interior of a covered pedestrian bridge in Ban Chang, Rayong Province, Thailand, showcasing its striking geometric steel framework. The structure features a repeating pattern of white-painted trusses with red accents along the ceiling beams, creating a tunnel-like perspective that draws the eye toward the far end of the walkway. Sunlight streams through the open sides of the bridge, casting intricate diagonal shadows from the angular supports across the tiled floor, producing a dramatic interplay of light and shade. Through the open sides, glimpses of greenery and distant buildings are visible, while the metal railings run parallel along both sides of the passage. The combination of industrial architecture, bold colors, and dynamic shadow patterns gives the scene a visually compelling, almost kaleidoscopic quality despite its utilitarian purpose.

ImageDescription.value:
Small fragment of a medieval (14th or 15th century) decorated floor tile. The fragment is broadly sub-rectangular consisting of one corner end of a much large square or rectangular tile. It measures 121.9mm length, 62.6mm width, is 26.1mm thick and weighs 349 grams. 
The fabric of the tile is relatively hard with a number of angular and sub-angular quartz (both abundant rose and infrequent white) iron stone and grit inclusions. The fabric is also mica rich. The fabric colour is a uniform mid orange brown. The upper surface of the tile has been decorated with a complex interlocking geometric pattern. It is likely that the design is from the centre of a four tile tessellating block as the linking design is positioned in one corner of the tile. The design in this corner seems to be based around a floral pattern, possibly having four (of which on survives fleur-de-lys or similar floral scrolls contained within a circular border. Adjacent, and outside of this border, is a further design consisting of interlocking S shapes forming a figure of eight border along one edge. All of these designs have been formed by impressing the surface of the tile with a die to create the pattern. The pattern is then filled with a white (usually pipe) clay wash that fills the stamped design. This has been further augmented by the application of a green coloured glaze / wash to the entire is upper surface. When fired this has produced a two tone green pattern present on this tile. Much of this surface has decayed and been lost and the pipe clay has deteriorated slightly and is now a mid buff / pale yellow colour. The original edges of the tile have a mid green brown glaze adhering to them suggesting that the tile was dipped and left to dry. There is no evidence of mortar on any of the surfaces of the tile. This suggests that they were laid either on a bed of sand or straight onto a leveled beaten earth floor. The upper surface with the design impressed upon it is smoother than the other faces and this might be a direct result of in situ wear. This style of two tone decorative floor tile is relatively common in both churches and high status secular buildings dating from the later medieval period 1300-1450.

ImageDescription.value:
Part of a medieval tile with stamped decoration. This may be part of a floor or wall-mounted tile, and consists of one right-angled corner with a border along both sides decorated with a row of ring and dot motifs made with a stamp 15.07mm in diameter. There are four such motifs in a row running up the tile, and three in a row along the base. The border measures 28.57mm in width along the base and c.49mm in width along the side of the tile. The border surrounds a central rectangular panel which is incomplete due to old breaks and is divided longitudinally by a narrow band 86.5mm long, 11mm in width at the base tapering to 8.5mm near the top broken edge.

To the left there is relief decoration depicting a standing figure with an elongated, triangular-shaped upper body, a belt, and a knee-length tunic from which the legs and feet emerge, facing right right. There is a neck at the top of the garment but the tile is broken off and the head is missing. Along the left side of the figure and within the panel is a zig-zag border of seven projecting triangles. To the right of the figure is an arm with a hand holding an object which may be the pommel of a sword whose blade descends to a point. This arm appears to be attached to the vertical band dividing the panel, and may have been mirrored to the right where a second possible sword can be seen, also having a round pommel, hilt and long blade. An alternative suggestion is that these objects represent fish rather than swords. Caryl Dane comments " The shapes reminded me of Alveston Manor 5 great square-headed brooch catch-piece, illustrated in Hines, 1997, Figure 49a and described as a fish-shape.

There is a rounded terminal at the top of the band. There are traces in the field of a yellow infil, presumably glaze or slip, and a darker slip or glaze is also suggested by a darker deposit on some parts of the surface of the tile. The width of the vertical border with ring and dot motifs suggests that the tile may originally have been quite wide and rectangular. Assuming a mirror-image from the vertical band, the complete tile would be 180mm wide. However, the figure that survives may have been flanking a larger composition, such as saint or biblical scene, assuming a church or monastic location, originally, for the tile. It could also be part of a larger scene composed of several separate tiles. The fragment measures 131.07mm in length, 144.11mm in width, 29mm in thickness, and weighs 700g.

David Sherlock's work on Medieval Suffolk floor tiles catalogues a wide range of designs none of which is quite like this. However some with geometric designs include ring and dot or concentric circles for example no.120 from Butley Priory and no.135 from Sudbury, St Peter. Its discovery at Oulton, close to the coast could indicate a continental source for its origins.

ImageDescription.value:
Sunlight drifts into this courtyard at Pena Palace, catching the patterned tiles and carved stone in a way that makes the entire space feel alive. Every surface seems to hold a different rhythm—azulejo mosaics wrapping the upper level, geometric tiles shifting across the floor, and sculpted columns rising like something pulled from a dream. The courtyard gathers all of these details and folds them into a single moment where Portugal’s history, craftsmanship, and imagination meet in the open air.

The contrast between the warm red exterior above and the cooler stonework below adds depth to the composition. Those bright walls anchor the palace’s Romantic spirit, while the tiles below speak to centuries of Moorish influence—math, pattern, and ornament expressed through color and repetition. Even the planters, carved and timeworn, feel like small sculptures placed intentionally to echo the drama of the architecture.

Standing here, it’s easy to feel the palace’s layered personality: part monastery, part royal retreat, part whimsical adventure in color and form. The courtyard becomes a kind of crossroads where every arch, shadow, and decorative flourish invites the eye to wander. It’s a quiet space filled with detail, a sheltered pause before stepping deeper into the palace’s kaleidoscope of styles.

ImageDescription.value: alt: Photo of a greenhouse interior. Various plants in pots and hanging baskets are arranged around a rectangular pool with a small fountain in the centre. The floor is tiled in a light beige colour with a darker geometric pattern. The walls are muted grey-green, and the glass ceiling and arched windows allow natural light to filter through; this light has a more orange hue caused by the pollution from wildfires. Hanging baskets containing ferns and other greenery are suspended from the ceiling. A metal chair is visible near the centre of the room, adding a touch of human presence to the otherwise natural setting. The atmosphere is calm and inviting, suggesting a peaceful retreat within the greenhouse.
